readerTitle: Why Aldi makes shopping a little harder on purpose
caseNote: 실제 기업 (Aldi) + 실제 연구 (Porter 1996) + 가상 적용 (급여 대행 회사, 사내 IT 지원팀)
insight: 트레이드오프는 약점이 아니라 방어막이다. 무언가를 포기해야 얻을 수 있는 위치는 경쟁자도 같은 것을 포기해야만 따라올 수 있다.
misconception: 좋은 전략이라면 품질, 가격, 서비스를 모두 잡을 수 있다. 무언가를 포기하는 것은 실행력이 부족하다는 뜻이다.

sources.text: Porter, M. (1996). What Is Strategy? Harvard Business Review. (trade-offs, straddling)
Aldi company websites (store format: own-label range, coin-deposit carts, shoppers bag their own groceries, products displayed in shipping cartons)
급여 대행 회사와 사내 IT 지원팀은 설명용 가상 사례

factChecks.note: Aldi의 코인 보증금 카트, 직접 장바구니 담기, 배송 박스째 진열, 자체 브랜드 중심 구성은 국가별로 운영이 다릅니다. 카드에는 "at many Aldi stores"로 적었습니다. 게시 전 Aldi 공식 자료로 다시 확인하세요.
Aldi의 취급 품목 수와 자체 브랜드 비중은 자료마다 수치가 달라 구체적인 숫자를 쓰지 않고 "a much smaller range, mostly own brands"로만 적었습니다.
Porter(1996)가 트레이드오프를 전략의 필수 조건으로 설명하고, 양쪽을 동시에 취하려는 시도를 "straddling"이라고 부른 점을 원문으로 확인하세요.

cards.title: Why Aldi makes shopping a little harder on purpose
body: At many Aldi stores, you put a coin in to unlock a cart. You bag your own groceries. Products sit on the shelf in the boxes they were shipped in, and most carry Aldi's own labels.
None of this is an accident. Each small inconvenience is a choice. Together, they help keep prices low.

image.label: Grocery shelf stocked with products in open shipping cartons
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 마트 선반에 상품이 배송용 골판지 박스째 놓여 있고, 앞쪽에 동전을 꽂는 카트와 직접 장바구니에 물건을 담는 손님. 실제 Aldi 로고나 상표, 실제 브랜드 포장은 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: Your biggest client ever wants something different.
body: You run a 12-person payroll firm for small businesses. One standard package, a low monthly fee, and every question answered within a day.
A 400-employee company will sign if you add a dedicated account manager and custom monthly reports. It would be your biggest client. What do you do?

options.text: Sign them and build the custom service
options.feedback: You win a big contract, but your best people get pulled into custom work. Response times slip for the small clients your low fee was built around.

options.text: Offer only the standard package, and accept they may walk
options.feedback: You may lose the deal, but you keep the speed and price your other clients came for. This lesson is about why that loss can be worth it.

options.text: Sign them at a premium price, served by the same team
options.feedback: The higher fee helps, but price doesn't create time. The same 12 people still have to serve two very different kinds of client.

cards.title: What Aldi gives up.
body: Compared with a typical large supermarket, Aldi accepts real costs:
list: **Less choice:** a much smaller range, mostly own brands. Some shoppers won't find their favorite.
**Less service:** no one bags for you, and you return your own cart.
**Less display:** cartons instead of carefully styled shelves.
cards.callout: In return: fewer items to stock, fewer staff hours, and lower prices.
cards.softwareNote: Software makes the same choices. A tool that offers fewer settings and no custom setup can ship faster and charge less, but it will lose customers who need everything tailored.

cards.title: Trade-offs
body: A **trade-off** is a choice where getting more of one thing means getting less of another. Low prices or wide choice. Speed or customization.
In his 1996 essay "What Is Strategy?", Michael Porter argued that real strategy needs trade-offs. If a position cost you nothing, any rival could take it too.
Aldi didn't fail at offering choice. It chose not to.

image.label: A balance scale: low prices on one side, wide choice and service on the other
image.brief: 플랫 일러스트 저울. 한쪽 접시에 "Low prices", 다른 쪽 접시에 "Wide choice", "Full service". 한쪽이 내려가면 다른 쪽이 올라가는 모습. 로고 없음.

cards.title: Why giving things up protects you.
body: Picture a big supermarket that wants Aldi's prices. It would have to cut its range and its service. But its loyal shoppers come *for* the range and service. Copying Aldi means losing them.
Porter called the half-way attempt **straddling**: adding a cheap option while keeping everything else. You carry the costs of both and fully satisfy neither group.
Your trade-off is the wall a rival has to climb.

cards.title: Not every trade-off is real.
body: Sometimes you can be faster *and* cheaper at once, by cutting waste or using better tools. That's efficiency, not strategy. Don't use "trade-off" as an excuse for sloppy work.
Trade-offs also shift. New technology can remove one that held for decades. Recheck yours every few years instead of treating it as a law.

cards.title: Now it's a team inside a company.
body: You lead an 8-person IT support team in a 2,000-person company. Staff love that you fix laptop and login problems within an hour.
The finance department now wants two of your people for a six-month systems project. Leadership says, "Do both." What do you do?

options.text: Agree and promise both the one-hour fixes and the project
options.feedback: It avoids a hard conversation today. But with two fewer people, fix times will slip, and everyone will feel let down by a promise you couldn't keep.

options.text: Show leadership the trade-off and ask them to choose what slows down
options.feedback: You turn a hidden cost into a visible decision. Whichever they pick, people know what to expect, and the choice is owned by those who set priorities.

options.text: Take the project quietly and let fix times drift
options.feedback: The project gets done, which may be right. But making the trade-off silently means staff discover it as bad service, not as a decision.

cards.title: A position worth having costs you something.
body: If your strategy gives up nothing, anyone can copy it. What you choose to be worse at is what protects what you're best at.
**Try it today:** finish this sentence about your business or team: "We are deliberately worse at ___ so we can be better at ___." If you can't fill it in, you may be straddling.
